mainTopic: Preparing food, fire and new vessels on יום טוב: testing versus hardening, and what counts as forbidden work
overview: The amud opens with two reasons why new tiles may not be heated on יום טוב: the heating either 'tests' them or 'hardens' them. Next the גמרא quotes a משנה about a crushed bird that lived twenty-four hours, and רבי אלעזר בר ינאי adds that it still needs checking. רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא whether such a doubtful bird may be slaughtered on יום טוב. רבי זירא tries to prove from the tiles that we do not do work on something that might turn out flawed. The reply is that the tile rule is about hardening, not testing, so the proof falls away. A ברייתא about several people cooking together on שבת leads ריש לקיש to explain that setting down a new pot is like heating new tiles. Then a series of ברייתות lists what may and may not be done on יום טוב with new ovens, meat, vegetables, fires, skewers, reeds and nuts. The amud ends as a new משנה of רבי אליעזר about מוקצה begins, continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: Two reasons why new tiles may not be heated on יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining the ban on heating tiles. One view says it is because they need to be tested. Another view says it is because they need to be hardened.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because one needs to test them. And some say: because one needs to harden them.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of an earlier discussion about heating tiles on יום טוב. The גמרא gives two possible reasons for the ban.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reason one: the first heating checks whether the tiles will crack. If they crack, the heating was useless work. Reason two: the first heating hardens the tiles and finishes them as cooking tools, which is like making a כלי on יום טוב.

keyTerms.meaning: to test them, to see whether the new tiles will crack
to harden them, to temper new tiles by strong heating

phrases.english: because it is necessary to test them.
phrases.notes: This is the tail end of the reason for not heating new tiles on יום טוב: the heating checks whether they'll crack.

phrases.english: And some say:
because it is necessary to harden them.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Heating new tiles on יום טוב is forbidden, either because it tests them or because it hardens them into usable tools.
steps.whyThisMatters: The first reason, 'testing', is the exact idea רבי זירא will use below to answer רבי ירמיה's question.

steps.title: The משנה of the crushed bird that survived a full day
steps.stepSummary: A משנה elsewhere rules that a bird that was trampled, thrown, or crushed, lived twenty-four hours, and was then slaughtered, is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned there: if one trampled it, or threw it against a wall, or an animal crushed it, and it is twitching, and it lived for twenty-four hours, and then he slaughtered it, it is kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings in a new source, a משנה from another מסכת, about a bird hurt by trampling or crushing. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An injury like this might have made the bird a טריפה. Surviving twenty-four hours shows it is not, so the bird is kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: twitching or struggling, but unable to stand
a full twenty-four hours, from one time to the same time the next day

phrases.english: We learned in a משנה there:
If one trampled it, or threw it against a wall,
phrases.notes: The 'it' is a bird. Here שטרפה means 'smashed it', not the word טריפה.

phrases.english: or an animal crushed it, and it is twitching,
and it lived on for twenty-four hours
and he slaughtered it, it is kosher.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A crushed bird that survives twenty-four hours and is then slaughtered is kosher.

steps.title: The bird still needs to be checked
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בר ינאי, quoting רבי אלעזר בן אנטיגנוס, adds that this bird must be checked after slaughtering.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בר ינאי said in the name of רבי אלעזר בן אנטיגנוס: it requires checking.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא adds a condition to the משנה: surviving one day is not enough, and the bird must also be checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of this added condition, the bird's kosher status is still uncertain when you go to slaughter it. It might still turn out to be a טריפה. That doubt is what makes the next question possible.

keyTerms.meaning: it needs checking, an inspection of the insides for damage

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai said
in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonus:
It requires checking.
phrases.notes: He means checking the bird after it is slaughtered, to make sure the injury didn't make it a טריפה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רבי אלעזר בר ינאי משום רבי אלעזר בן אנטיגנוס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a condition to the משנה's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even after surviving twenty-four hours, the crushed bird must be checked before it is considered kosher.

steps.title: May this doubtful bird be slaughtered on יום טוב?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי זירא whether the crushed bird may be slaughtered on יום טוב, since it might turn out to have a defect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked רבי זירא: what is the law about slaughtering it on יום טוב? Do we assume on יום טוב that it has a defect, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the question of the section is asked: since the bird needs checking, may we slaughter it on יום טוב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the bird turns out to be a טריפה, the slaughtering was work done for nothing on יום טוב. So the question is whether we worry that the bird is damaged and forbid slaughtering it, or assume it is fine and allow it.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי זֵירָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira:
What is the law about slaughtering it on יום טוב?

phrases.aramaic: מִי מַחְזְקִינַן רֵעוּתָא בְּיוֹם טוֹב, אוֹ לָא?
phrases.english: Do we presume a defect on יום טוב, or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: בעא מיניה רבי ירמיה מרבי זירא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the rule that the bird needs checking to ask about יום טוב.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: On יום טוב, do we worry that a bird of doubtful status may be flawed and forbid slaughtering it, or not?

steps.title: רבי זירא answers from the case of the new tiles
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא points to the rule against heating new tiles on יום טוב, which רבי יוחנן explained as being because they need to be tested. So too, we do not do work on something that might turn out to be flawed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: we already learned it. One may not whiten tiles in order to roast on them. And we discussed it: what is he doing wrong? And רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: here we are dealing with new tiles, because he needs to test them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers by quoting an earlier ruling about tiles and its explanation. He is using it as proof that the bird may not be slaughtered on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: New tiles might crack when heated, which would make the heating useless. Even so, חכמים forbade it on יום טוב. In the same way, slaughtering a bird that might be a טריפה risks useless work, so it should be forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: tiles used as a surface for roasting
and we discussed it, raising a question about it
here we are dealing with a specific case

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא tries to prove that on יום טוב we do not do a מלאכה on something whose usefulness is still in doubt, using the new tiles that still need testing. The next step rejects this proof, so do not treat it as the final ruling.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not just a repeat of step 1. רבי זירא brings back the 'testing' reason on purpose, to use it as proof for the bird question.

phrases.english: He said to him: We have already learned it:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מְלַבְּנִין אֶת הָרְעָפִים לִצְלוֹת בָּהֶן.
phrases.english: One may not whiten tiles in order to roast on them.
phrases.notes: 'Whiten' means heating them until they glow white-hot.

phrases.english: And we discussed it: what is he doing wrong?

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
Here we are dealing with new tiles,
because he needs to test them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 4 by comparing it to the tile ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: We do worry about a defect on יום טוב. Just as untested tiles may not be heated, a bird that still needs checking should not be slaughtered.
steps.raayaObject: That on יום טוב one may not do work on something that might turn out flawed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling 'אין מלבנין את הרעפים' as explained by רבי יוחנן: new tiles need testing.

steps.title: The tile rule is about hardening, not testing
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה rejects רבי זירא's proof. The tile rule is based on hardening the tiles, which has nothing to do with checking a bird.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We learn that rule as being because the tiles need to be hardened.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה pushes back on רבי זירא's answer. He holds that the tile ban is about hardening the tiles, not about testing them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא's proof only works if the tile ban is about testing, like the bird needs testing. If the ban is really about hardening the tiles, which finishes making a usable כלי, then it has nothing to do with the bird. So the proof falls away, and there is no reason here to forbid slaughtering the bird on יום טוב.

keyTerms.meaning: to harden them (finishing them as usable vessels)
we learn / we teach (the reason this way)

steps.whatToRemember: The two reasons from Step 1 now matter: 'testing' would support forbidding the bird, while 'hardening' does not.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רבי ירמיה answering רבי זירא.

phrases.english: We, "because one needs to harden them"
phrases.notes: He means the tiles from Step 1, the second reason given there.

phrases.english: is how we learn it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנַן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְחׇסְמָן מַתְנִינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer offered in Step 5 by holding a different reason for the tile rule.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the crushed bird and heating new tiles.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The tile rule is about hardening (making a כלי), not about testing, so it says nothing about the bird.

steps.title: Several people cooking together are all liable
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that when six people each do part of the cooking on שבת, all of them are liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: One brings the fire, one brings the wood, one sets the pot on the stove, one brings the water, one puts in spices, and one stirs. All of them are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It describes a group sharing one act of cooking, and it rules that every one of them is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person does only one part of the cooking, yet each is counted as a cook. This ברייתא will soon be challenged, and its 'pot-setter' will connect back to the topic of tiles.

keyTerms.meaning: sets the pot on the stove

phrases.english: It was taught: One brings the fire,
phrases.notes: This is about cooking on שבת.

phrases.english: and one brings the wood,
and one sets the pot on the stove,
and one brings the water,
and one puts spices into it,
and one stirs: they are all liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new source, which will later link back to the tile topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When several people share the act of cooking on שבת, all are liable.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says only the last one is liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a different ברייתא that says only the last person is liable and everyone else is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: The last one is liable and all the rest are exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from Step 7 with another ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 makes everyone liable. This ברייתא makes only the final person liable. Both cannot be true in the same case, so the גמרא needs to explain the difference.

phrases.english: But it was taught: The last one is liable
and all the rest are exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 7 with a contradicting ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in Step 7 that all participants are liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא says only the last participant is liable, which contradicts the first.

steps.title: It depends on when the fire was brought
steps.stepSummary: If the fire was brought first, everyone after it is helping cook, so all are liable. If the fire was brought last, only that person cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This ברייתא is where he brought the fire at the start. That ברייתא is where he brought the fire at the end.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by placing each ברייתא in a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cooking only begins once there is fire. If the fire came first, every later step adds to real cooking, so all are liable. If the fire came last, the earlier people only prepared things, and only the one who brought the fire actually cooked.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where he brought fire at the start,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the ברייתא where everyone is liable.

phrases.english: that is where he brought fire at the end.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּאַיְיתִי אוּר מֵעִיקָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting into two different cases (הָא בְּ... הָא בְּ...)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to argue about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: All are liable when the fire came first. Only the last is liable when the fire came last.

steps.title: What did the pot-setter actually do?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the person who only set the pot on the stove did any forbidden work.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that all the others did an action. But the one who sets the pot on the stove, what has he done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא from Step 7. Setting a pot down does not seem to be any part of cooking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bringing fire, wood, water, or spices, or stirring, all help the food cook. Placing a pot on the stove does not seem to add any real work, so why is that person liable?

phrases.english: Granted, all of them did an action,
but the one who sets the pot on the stove,
what has he done?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא כּוּלְּהוּ קָא עָבְדִי מַעֲשֶׂה, אֶלָּא שׁוֹפֵת אֶת הַקְּדֵרָה מַאי קָא עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to Step 7 and questions one of the people listed there.
steps.kashyaTarget: The liability of the שׁוֹפֵת אֶת הַקְּדֵרָה in Step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setting a pot on the stove does not seem to be a forbidden action at all.

steps.title: A new pot is like heating new tiles
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the case is a new pot. Setting it on the fire hardens it, just like heating new tiles.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: Here we are dealing with a new pot, and they applied the rule of heating tiles to it.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש answers the question from Step 10. The pot-setter is liable because placing a new pot on the fire hardens the pot itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His liability is not for cooking the food but for finishing the pot, the same way heating new tiles finishes them. This ties the ברייתא back to the tile topic from Step 1.
steps.confusionAlert: The pot-setter is not liable for cooking the food. He is liable for hardening the new pot.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that hardening a new כלי with fire is itself forbidden work, which supports the 'hardening' reason for the tile rule.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
Here we are dealing with a new pot,
and because of heating tiles they touched on it.
phrases.notes: He means they gave the new pot the same rule as heating new tiles.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ: הָכָא בִּקְדֵרָה חֲדָשָׁה עָסְקִינַן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case narrowly (a new pot)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Setting a pot down seemed to involve no forbidden work.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a new pot, the fire hardens it like tiles, so placing it counts as forbidden work.

steps.title: What may be done to new ovens and stoves on יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: New ovens and stoves may be moved like other vessels. But you may not oil them, rub them, or cool them to harden them. If it is done in order to bake, it is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: New ovens and stoves are like all vessels that may be carried in a courtyard. But one may not smear them with oil, rub them with a rag, or cool them with cold water to harden them. If it is in order to bake, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with rules for new ovens and stoves on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You may move them, but you may not do things that finish and strengthen them, since that is making a כלי. The exception is narrow: if the oven is too hot, you may cool it with water so the bread will not burn, since that is for baking. It is not a general permission to oil, rub or harden a new oven.
steps.whatToRemember: Hardening a new oven on יום טוב is forbidden. The only exception is cooling an oven that is too hot, so the bread will not burn.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: New ovens and stoves
are like all vessels
that may be carried in a courtyard.
But one may not smear them with oil,
nor rub them with a rag,
nor cool them with cold water
in order to harden them,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם בִּשְׁבִיל לֶאֱפוֹת — הֲרֵי זֶה מוּתָּר.
phrases.english: and if it is in order to bake, this is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new ברייתא on the related theme of hardening new vessels.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oiling, rubbing or cooling new ovens and stoves to harden them on יום טוב is forbidden, but cooling an oven that is too hot to bake in without burning the bread is allowed.

steps.title: Removing hair from the head and feet of an animal
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says you may scald or singe the hair off an animal's head and feet on יום טוב. You may not smear them with clay, earth or lime, and you may not cut the hair with scissors.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: you may put the head and feet in hot water and singe them in the fire to get the hair off. But you may not smear them with clay, earth or lime, and you may not cut the hair with scissors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא listing which ways of getting hair off meat are allowed on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Scalding and singeing are simple ways of getting the meat ready to eat, so they are allowed. Smearing with clay, earth or lime takes much more effort. Cutting the hair with scissors looks like shearing, which is ordinary weekday work.

keyTerms.meaning: Scald with hot water to loosen the hair

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One may scald the head and the feet
and one may singe them in the fire,
but one may not smear them with clay,
nor with earth, nor with lime.
And one may not shear them with scissors.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מוֹלְגִין אֶת הָרֹאשׁ וְאֶת הָרַגְלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of Step 12, which listed what may and may not be done to prepare things for יום טוב cooking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scalding and singeing hair off meat is allowed on יום טוב. Smearing with clay, earth or lime, or shearing with scissors, is not.

steps.title: Vegetables, bitter greens and baking ovens
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues. You may not trim vegetables with their special shears, but you may prepare קונדס and עכביות. You may bake in a פורני and heat water in an אנטיכי, but you may not bake in a new פורני in case it breaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: You may not trim a vegetable with its special shears. But you may prepare קונדס and עכביות. You may light and bake in a big oven and heat water in an urn. But you may not bake in a new big oven, because it might crack.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues its list with rules about vegetables and about large ovens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trimming with the special shears is treated like the scissors in Step 13, a weekday way of working. Preparing hard bitter greens is allowed even though it takes effort. A new oven is forbidden for a different reason: if it cracks, the work was done for nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The special shears used for trimming vegetables
Kinds of bitter plants that take a lot of preparing
A large urn for heating water
In case it breaks or cracks

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think every big effort is forbidden. Preparing קונדס is a lot of work and is still allowed. The problems here are weekday-style tools and the risk of wasted work.

phrases.english: And one may not trim the vegetable
with its special shears.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְתַקְּנִין אֶת הַקּוּנְדָּס וְאֶת הָעַכָּבִיּוֹת,
phrases.english: But one may prepare kundas and akaviyot,
phrases.notes: These are bitter plants that are only good to eat after a lot of preparing.

phrases.english: and one may light a fire and bake in a large oven,
and one may heat water in an urn,
but one may not bake in a new large oven
in case it breaks.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין גּוֹזְזִין אֶת הַיָּרָק בַּתִּסְפּוֹרֶת שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the second half of the same ברייתא. Its ban on a new oven 'in case it breaks' (שמא תפחת) echoes the 'testing' concern from Steps 1 and 5. Steps 11-12 were about hardening, which is a different concern.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trimming vegetables with their shears is forbidden. Preparing hard greens, baking in a פורני and heating water in an אנטיכי are allowed. Baking in a new פורני is forbidden because it might crack.

steps.title: Blowing on a fire and fixing a skewer
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says you may not blow on a fire with bellows, but you may with a tube. You may not fix or sharpen a skewer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: you may not blow on a fire with bellows, but you may blow through a tube. You may not fix a skewer, and you may not sharpen it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא about getting the fire and cooking tools ready on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bellows are the normal weekday tool for blowing on a fire, so they are not allowed. A tube is an unusual way to do it, so it is allowed. Fixing or sharpening a skewer is repairing a tool, not preparing food, so it is forbidden.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One may not blow on a fire with bellows,
but one may blow with a tube.
And one may not fix a skewer,
and one may not sharpen it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another ברייתא with the same pattern: the normal weekday way is forbidden, and an unusual or direct food-serving way is allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using bellows is forbidden and using a tube is allowed. Fixing or sharpening a skewer is forbidden.

steps.title: Splitting a reed and cracking a nut
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says you may not split a reed to use it for roasting salted fish. But you may crack a nut wrapped in a cloth, and you need not worry that the cloth might tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: you may not split a reed to roast salted fish on it. But you may crack a nut inside a cloth, and you do not need to worry that the cloth will tear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more ברייתא, comparing making a tool, which is forbidden, with cracking food, which is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting a reed turns it into a new tool, a kind of skewer, so it is not allowed. Cracking a nut is preparing the food itself. Even if the cloth tears, no forbidden work was done, so we are not worried about it.
steps.whatToRemember: Across these ברייתות, simple acts that directly prepare the food are allowed on יום טוב. Making or fixing tools, weekday-style methods and work that might be wasted are not allowed.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין מְפַצְּעִין אֶת הַקָּנֶה
phrases.english: The Sages taught: One may not split a reed
to roast salted fish on it,
but one may crack a nut in a cloth,
and we do not worry that it might tear.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין מְפַצְּעִין אֶת הַקָּנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the list of ברייתות about preparing food and tools on יום טוב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Splitting a reed to make a skewer is forbidden. Cracking a nut in a cloth is allowed, with no concern about tearing the cloth.

steps.title: New משנה: רבי אליעזר on standing by set-aside produce
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. רבי אליעזר gives another lenient ruling: a person may stand near produce that is מוקצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: רבי אליעזר also said: a person may stand over produce that was set aside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts a new משנה. This line only opens רבי אליעזר's ruling, and the rest continues in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ועוד, 'and also', tells us this is one more lenient ruling from רבי אליעזר after his earlier ones in this chapter. The topic now switches from cooking methods to produce that was set aside, called מוקצה.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, our משנה. It marks the start of a new משנה.
And he also said. This adds another ruling from the same Sage.
Here, produce that was set aside and not meant for use

phrases.english: MISHNA: And Rabbi Eliezer also said:
A person may stand over produce that was set aside

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתות about food preparation and opens a new משנה on a different topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר begins a lenient ruling allowing a person to stand over מוקצה produce. The rest of the ruling continues in the next section.
